english.html: to make it evident that such an obligation was contracted. Nevertheless it has the effect and force of a bequest: that is to say, the heir may be compelled to pay the said hundred écus, if not as owed, at least as left by legacy or fideicommissum k. Except in two cases. The first, when it should appear that such confession had been made by error and imprudently l; for then there is no consent or will of the disposer m, inasmuch as, as Ulpian says, there is nothing so contrary to consent as the error which clearly discovers the imprudence and simplicity of the speaker n. The second, when such confession should be made in favour of a person to whom the law forbids, or does not permit, that anything, or very little, be left o; because it is then to be presumed, and very likely, that such acknowledgment was made to defraud the law and its intention p, which by this means could always be frustrated and annulled. As (by way of example) if someone wished to leave to his second wife more than is permitted him by the law of Justinian, that is to say, more than to one of the children of the first marriage q, and in his testament confessed to have received from his said wife a thousand écus: such confession, although the testator husband should assure by a thousand oaths that it was true, would profit nothing r. And as to saying that the confession of a debt, made by the testator and fortified by oath, makes sufficient proof ſ: that is understood where deceit and fraud are absent; for the religion of the oath gives no authority to a wicked and fraudulent act t. Now when the confession is made in favour of a person incapable by law, the fraud is patent u. Nor is it anything to say that a gift made between married persons (such as the said acknowledgment may be called), although invalid, is nevertheless confirmed not only by the silence and death of the donor x, but also by oath. For the difference is very great between the oath which is interposed upon a gift and that which intervenes upon an acknowledgment: inasmuch as the former intervenes upon what is to come — for he

tee. Toutesfois elle a effect, & vertu de laiz: c'eſt à dire,
que l'heritier pourra eſtre contraint de payer leſdits
cent eſcus, ſi non comme deuz au moins comme laiſſez
par legat, ou fideicommis {k}. Si ce n'eſt en deux cas:
Le premier, quand il apparoiſtroit telle confeſſiõ auoir
eſté par erreur & imprudemment faite {l}. Car alors n'y
a aucun conſentement, ou volonré du diſpoſant {m}.
d'autant que comme dit Vlpien, il n'y a rien ſi cõtraire
au conſentemẽt, que l'erreur qui deſcouure clairemẽt
l'imprudence, & la ſimplicité de celuy qui parle {n}. Le
ſecond, quand telle confeſſion ſeroit faite au profit de
la perſonne, à laquelle le droit defend, ou ne permet
laiſſer riẽ, ou bien peu {o}. partãt qu'il eſt lors a preſumer
& fort vray ſemblable, que telle reeognoiſſance a e-
ſté faite pour frauder la loy, & ſon intention {p}: laquel-
le par ce moyen pourroit eſtre touſiouts fruſtree, & a-

vouloit laiſſer à ſa ſeconde femme, plus qu'il ne luy eſt
permis par la loy de Iuſtiniẽ. C'eſt à dire, plus que à vn
des enfans du premier mariage {q}. Et en ſon teſtamẽt, cõ
feſſoit auoir receu de ſadite femme mille eſcus: telle
confeſſion, biẽ que le mari teſtateur l'aſſeuraſt par mil-
le ſermens eſtre veritable; ne profiteroit rien {r}. Et de di-
re que la confeſſion d'vne debte, faite par le teſtateur,
fortifiee de ſerment, fait preuue ſuffiſante {ſ}. Cela ſ'entẽd,
dol & fraude ceſſans: Car la religion du ſerment ne dõ
ne point d'authorité à vn acte mauuais, & frauduleux
{t}. Or quand la confeſſion eſt faite, au profit de perſon

fait rien auſſi dire, qu'vne donaiſon faite entre les ma-
riez (telle que peut eſtre appellee ladite recognoiſſan

non ſeulemẽt par ſilẽce, & mort du donateur {x}: mais en
core auſſi par ſermẽt. Car la differẽce eſt fort grãde en-
tre le ſermẽt, qui eſt interpoſé ſur vne donaiſon, & ce-

premier interuient ſur ce qu'eſt à aduenir, Car celuy
